title: Faruk Patel Built a Rs 10,964 Crore Green Energy Empire From Rs 1 Lakh
excerpt: The son of a bus conductor who once drove an auto and worked at Pizza Hut, Dr Faruk G. Patel built KP Group from a Rs 1 lakh trucking venture in 1994 into one of India's leading solar and wind conglomerates.
body:
• Dr Faruk G. Patel, a bus conductor's son from Surat, started the KP Group in 1994 with Rs 1 lakh of savings; the conglomerate's listed businesses are now valued at roughly Rs 10,964 crore, according to India Today's profile.
  • Two group companies are publicly traded: KPI Green Energy (solar) on the NSE and BSE, and KP Energy (wind) on the BSE — KP Energy made Forbes Asia's Best Under a Billion list in 2024, with revenue rising from Rs 74 crore in FY20 to Rs 469 crore in FY24.
  • The KP Group now spans 18 companies employing over 2,500 people, and has set a target of installing 1,000 MW of renewable energy projects.
  • Patel's authorised biography, Urja No Ujaas (The Radiance of Energy), is out in Gujarati and English, with an audiobook version on Spotify — a rare documented playbook for first-generation Indian entrepreneurs.

Opening news lead

Before he ran a renewable energy conglomerate, Faruk Patel drove an auto-rickshaw and worked at Pizza Hut to make ends meet. Three decades on, the Surat entrepreneur who founded the KP Group in 1994 with just Rs 1 lakh of his own savings now leads a green energy empire whose businesses are valued at Rs 10,964 crore, according to an India Today feature profiling his journey. A newly released biography, Urja No Ujaas (The Radiance of Energy), documents the three-decade arc from a small trucking operation in Gujarat to one of India's leading renewable energy groups.

Context & Background

Patel was born into a modest Muslim family in Surat; his father was a bus conductor. After schooling at Surat Municipal Corporation school and later V.D. Desai Vadiwala School, he moved to Mumbai to learn the import-export trade, working as an optician on the side, and later earned a diploma in textile engineering from the Manmade Textile Research Association (MANTRA). In 1993, he ran a small carting business moving materials between Hazira and Bharuch; the savings funded the launch of KP Group a year later. The name KP comes from his native village, Kothi, and his surname.

The group's first act was pure logistics: KP Transport ran a fleet of trucks between Surat, Hajira, Bharuch and Jamnagar, building contracts with industrial clients including L&T and Reliance. In 1999–2001 came the pivot to construction and telecom, when KP Buildcon (now KP Green Engineering) began fabricating and installing mobile towers for Vodafone and Airtel, expanding to 16 states. The decisive turn came in 2008, as the telecom business slowed: Patel launched KPI Green Energy for solar and then KP Energy for wind, betting that the sun and the wind would outlast every business cycle. The group now counts 18 companies and employs more than 2,500 people directly and indirectly.

Impact & Analysis

The renewable bet paid off handsomely. KP Energy, listed on the BSE SME platform in 2016 with a market capitalisation of Rs 24.26 crore, grew to roughly Rs 2,620 crore by August 2024 and earned a place on Forbes Asia's Best Under a Billion list. The company has erected more than 545 wind turbines, provides end-to-end balance-of-plant infrastructure for wind and hybrid projects, and operates as an independent power producer. Recent wealth estimates, reported by Bhaskar English, put Patel's net worth past Rs 20,000 crore, making him Surat's richest industrialist ahead of the city's diamond tycoons — a symbolic changing of the guard in a city long defined by diamonds and textiles.

Analysts note the group rode two structural tailwinds: India's corporate demand for captive renewable power and the government's push for hybrid wind-solar capacity. KPI Green Energy, now on both the NSE and BSE main boards, develops solar parks for industrial consumers, while KP Energy holds an order book exceeding 1 GW. The trajectory mirrors India's broader energy transition — but from a founder with no inherited capital, no overseas degree and no institutional backing at the start.

"Every strategy I talk about has been planned two to three years ago. We have the data and we as a team decide which goals to achieve and when. That's the reason behind our success."

— Faruk G. Patel, CMD, KP Group, to The CEO Magazine

Diaspora Angle

The story resonates well beyond Gujarat. Urja No Ujaas, authored by UK-based writer Imtiaz Patel Varediwala of Blackburn, is available in Gujarati and English and as an audiobook on Spotify, giving diaspora readers a rare documented case study of a first-generation Indian entrepreneur scaling with no safety net. For NRIs weighing a return to India or investing back home, Patel's path — logistics to towers to solar — is a practical counter to the notion that Indian renewable ventures are the preserve of large industrial houses. His philanthropy, from hosting wedding celebrations with specially-abled children to funding education initiatives, also offers a template for diaspora giving tied to hometown causes.

What's Next

KP Group's stated ambition is to install 1,000 MW of renewable energy projects, a pledge Patel first made publicly around 2020, and the group is now pushing into green hydrogen — which he calls the fuel of the future. With India targeting 500 GW of non-fossil capacity by 2030, the group's hybrid wind-solar pipeline and its NTPC-linked projects position it to keep compounding. Whether the group can sustain its torrid growth as competition intensifies in India's renewable auction market will be the next test of the bus conductor's son's instincts.
